outcomes.text: Stain animal and plant cells and examine them under a microscope.
Draw labelled diagrams of the cells you observed.
Pick out ribosomes, mitochondria, nucleus, cytoplasm and membrane on animal cell images.
Pick out chloroplasts, sap vacuole and cellulose cell wall as well, on plant cell images.
Describe a bacterial cell: ribosomes, circular DNA, plasmids, cytoplasm, membrane and wall.
Say what each of these cell structures does in animal, plant and bacterial cells.

subtopics.title: Specialised cells and levels of organisation

outcomes.text: Understand that specialised cells have structures that suit their jobs.
Use the terms cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism correctly with examples.
State and use the formula magnification = image size divided by actual size.

topics.title: 2.1 Concept and use of a classification system

outcomes.text: Understand that organisms are sorted into groups by shared features.
Describe a species as organisms able to breed and produce fertile offspring.
Describe binomial naming, with a genus part and a species part.
Build and use dichotomous keys from visible features.
State the main features that place organisms in the animal, plant, fungus, prokaryote or protoctist kingdom.
State the features of vertebrate groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and arthropod groups (myriapods, insects, arachnids, crustaceans).
State the features of ferns and of flowering plants (dicots and monocots).
Classify organisms using the features from the previous three statements.
State the main features of viruses: a protein coat and genetic material.
Understand that viruses can only replicate inside living cells.

units.title: 3 Movement into and out of cells

outcomes.text: Describe water as a solvent in digestion, excretion and transport.
Understand that random kinetic energy of molecules and ions powers diffusion and osmosis.
Understand diffusion as net movement down a concentration gradient because of random motion.
Investigate how surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance affect diffusion.
Understand osmosis as net water movement from higher to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
Understand that water pressure inside cells pushes on the cell wall and supports plants.
Describe osmosis effects on plant and animal tissues, and the role of the water potential gradient in water uptake and loss.
Investigate plant tissues in different concentrations, using turgid, turgor pressure, plasmolysis and flaccid.
Investigate osmosis with materials such as dialysis tubing.
Understand active transport as movement against a concentration gradient through the membrane using energy from respiration.
Explain why active transport matters for ion uptake by root hair cells.
List the chemical elements in carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and DNA.
State that large molecules are built from smaller ones: starch, cellulose, glycogen from glucose; proteins from amino acids; lipids from fatty acids and glycerol; DNA from nucleotides.
Describe and carry out tests for starch, glucose and maltose, protein and lipids.
Describe a catalyst as speeding up a reaction without being changed.
Describe enzymes as protein biological catalysts involved in all metabolic reactions.
Explain enzyme action using substrate, active site, enzyme-substrate complex and product.
Explain enzyme specificity through the matching shape of the active site (lock and key).
Understand that reactions can be followed by measuring reactant and product concentrations.
Investigate and describe how temperature and pH change enzyme activity.
Explain these effects using kinetic energy, shape and fit, denaturation and collision frequency.
Understand photosynthesis as making carbohydrates from raw materials using light energy.
State that chlorophyll is a green pigment found in chloroplasts.
State that chlorophyll converts light energy into chemical energy for making glucose and other carbohydrates.
Outline how photosynthesis products are used and stored: starch, cellulose, respiration, sucrose.
State the word equation and balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.
Investigate the need for chlorophyll, light and carbon dioxide, using suitable controls.
Describe and explain how light, carbon dioxide and temperature change the rate of photosynthesis.
Investigate these factors using water plants and hydrogencarbonate indicator.
Identify and explain limiting factors of photosynthesis in different conditions.

subtopics.title: The leaf as a photosynthesis organ

outcomes.text: State that leaves are broad and thin, and explain how this helps photosynthesis.
Label a dicot leaf's cuticle, stomata, guard cells, mesophyll, air spaces, vascular bundles, chloroplasts and epidermis, and explain how each is adapted.
Explain why nitrate ions are needed to make amino acids and proteins.
Explain why magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll.

topics.title: 7.1 Uptake and transport of water and ions

outcomes.text: Relate root hair cell structure to water and ion uptake.
Outline the water route through root hair cells, cortex, xylem and mesophyll cells.
Use a stain to investigate the water pathway in a cut stem.
Describe transpiration as water vapour loss from leaves.
Understand that water evaporates from mesophyll surfaces and diffuses out through the stomata.
Explain how wind, temperature, humidity and light affect transpiration rate, and how wilting happens.
Investigate how wind speed, light and temperature affect transpiration rate.
Explain upward water movement in xylem through transpiration pull and attraction between water molecules.
Describe translocation as phloem movement of sucrose and amino acids from sources to sinks.
Locate xylem, phloem and cortex in sections of non-woody dicot roots and stems.
State that xylem carries water and mineral ions and gives support.
Relate xylem vessel structure to function: lignin walls, no contents, end-to-end tubes.
List sources and dietary importance of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins C and D, calcium, iron, fibre and water.
Name deficiency diseases and symptoms: scurvy, rickets (vitamin D and calcium) and anaemia.
Understand what a balanced diet is.
Identify the main regions of the digestive system, including duodenum, ileum, colon, rectum and anus.
Explain why most foods must be digested before absorption.
Describe physical digestion as breaking food into smaller pieces without chemical change.
Describe chemical digestion as breaking large molecules into small ones.
State that physical digestion increases surface area for enzymes.
Identify incisors, canines, premolars and molars.
Describe tooth structure: enamel, dentine, pulp, nerves and cement, set in the gum.
Describe what each type of tooth does in physical digestion.
Describe the functions of the mouth, salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, ileum, colon, rectum and anus.
Describe amylase, maltase, protease and lipase with their substrates and end-products.
Describe hydrochloric acid in the stomach as killing swallowed bacteria.
Understand that stomach and duodenum proteases work best at different pH levels.
Outline how bile emulsifies fats to speed up lipase digestion.
Describe peristalsis as waves of muscle contraction that move food along.
State that nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
Understand absorption as movement of nutrients from the intestine into the blood, by diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Understand assimilation as cells taking up and using nutrients from the blood.
Describe villus structure and the roles of capillaries and lacteals.
Explain how villi and microvilli increase the ileum's surface area.
Understand that water is absorbed in the small intestine and colon, mostly in the small intestine.
State that the hepatic portal vein carries most absorbed molecules and ions to the liver.
Describe human gas exchange surfaces: large area, thin, good blood and air supply.
State the percentages of gases in atmospheric air.
Investigate and explain differences between inspired and expired air.
Identify the larynx, trachea, lungs, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and capillaries.
State the features and role of the alveoli as the exchange surface.
Identify ribs, intercostal muscles and the diaphragm.
Explain how ribs, intercostal muscles and diaphragm change thorax volume and pressure to move air.
Investigate and explain how exercise changes breathing rate and depth.
Explain how goblet cells, cilia and mucus protect the gas exchange system.
Describe respiration as chemical reactions in all living cells that release energy from glucose.
State the uses of energy: muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, growth, nerve impulses and keeping body temperature steady.
Investigate and describe how temperature affects respiration in yeast.
Describe aerobic respiration as releasing a lot of energy by breaking down glucose with oxygen.
State the word and balanced chemical equations for aerobic respiration.
Describe anaerobic respiration as releasing little energy from glucose without oxygen.
State the word equation for anaerobic respiration in humans.
State the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
Explain why lactic acid builds up in vigorous exercise, causing an oxygen debt (EPOC).
Outline how the debt is repaid: fast heart rate carries lactic acid to the liver, deeper breathing supplies oxygen to break it down.
Describe the circulatory system as vessels, a pump and valves giving one-way blood flow.
Describe double circulation as blood passing through the heart twice per circuit.
Understand that double circulation gives low pressure to the lungs and high pressure to the body.
Identify the heart's muscular wall, septum, ventricles, atria, valves and coronary arteries.
Explain the different muscle wall thicknesses of the ventricles and of atria versus ventricles.
Describe a heartbeat: atria and ventricles contracting and the valves acting.
State that arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it.
State that heart activity is monitored by ECG, pulse rate and listening to valve sounds.
Investigate and explain how physical activity changes heart rate.
Describe coronary heart disease as blocked coronary arteries and list its risk factors.
Discuss how diet and exercise reduce the risk of coronary heart disease.
Name the main vessels to and from the heart, lungs, liver and kidneys.
Describe and identify the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries: wall thickness, wall composition, lumen and valves.
Explain how vessel structure relates to the blood pressure carried.
Identify red cells and white cells (lymphocytes and phagocytes) on slides and images.
List the components of blood: red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.
State the functions of red cells, white cells, platelets (clotting) and plasma (transport).
Describe how substances pass between capillary blood, tissue fluid and body cells.
Describe a pathogen as a disease-causing organism.
Describe a transmissible disease as one whose pathogen passes from host to host.
Understand that pathogens spread by direct contact or indirectly through surfaces, food, animals or air.
Describe the body's barriers: skin, nose hairs, mucus and stomach acid.
Understand the mosquito as a disease vector.
Describe the malaria parasite and how it is transmitted.
Describe controlling the malaria mosquito using its life cycle.
Explain that HIV is a viral pathogen.
Describe how HIV is transmitted.
Understand that HIV infection may lead to AIDS.
Describe ways HIV can be controlled.
Describe cholera as a bacterial disease spread by contaminated water.
Explain how clean water, hygiene, waste disposal and sewage treatment control cholera.
Explain how the cholera toxin causes chloride secretion, osmotic water loss, diarrhoea and dehydration.
Describe the effects of excessive alcohol: poor self-control, depressant, slow reactions, liver damage and social harm.
Describe the effects of tobacco smoke (nicotine, tar, carbon monoxide) on health and on birth weight.
Describe a drug as any substance that changes chemical reactions in the body.
Describe antibiotics as treatment for bacterial infection.
State that antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses.
Explain how using antibiotics only when essential limits resistant bacteria, including MRSA.
Describe active immunity as defence by the body's own antibody production.
State that each pathogen has its own antigens with specific shapes.
Describe antibodies as proteins that bind antigens, destroying pathogens or marking them for phagocytes.
State that antibodies have shapes complementary to specific antigens.
Explain that active immunity comes from infection or vaccination.
Outline vaccination: weakened pathogens or antigens, an immune response, and memory cells for long-term immunity.
Explain how vaccination controls transmissible diseases.
Explain passive immunity as short-term defence from another person's antibodies, via the placenta and breast milk.
Explain why breast-feeding matters for infants' passive immunity.
State that passive immunity produces no memory cells.
Outline how HIV weakens immunity: fewer lymphocytes and less antibody production.
Describe excretion as removing toxic materials and metabolic waste.
State that carbon dioxide from respiration is excreted by the lungs.
State that urea is a toxic waste made in the liver from excess amino acids.
Identify the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra and state each function.
Explain the need for excretion, limited to urea toxicity.
Outline nephron structure: Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, tubules, loop of Henle and collecting duct.
Outline nephron function: filtration, reabsorption and the formation of urine.
Describe the liver's role in assimilating amino acids into proteins.
Describe deamination as removing the nitrogen part of amino acids to form urea.
State that the nervous system coordinates and regulates body functions.
Describe the central and peripheral nervous systems.
Identify sensory, relay and motor neurones on diagrams.
State that electrical impulses travel along neurones.
Describe a simple reflex arc: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone and effector.
Describe a reflex action as a rapid automatic response to a stimulus.
Describe a synapse as a junction between two neurones.
Describe synapse structure: vesicles of neurotransmitter, the gap and receptor proteins.
Describe the events at a synapse from impulse arrival to a new impulse.
State that synapses make impulses travel in one direction only.
Describe sense organs as receptor cell groups responding to specific stimuli.
Identify the structures of the eye, from cornea to blind spot.
Describe the function of each part of the eye.
Explain the pupil reflex using circular and radial iris muscles.
Explain accommodation for near and distant objects.
Describe a hormone as a chemical from a gland, carried in blood, that changes target organs.
Identify endocrine glands and state the hormones they produce.
Understand how adrenaline raises blood glucose and heart rate, with example situations.
Compare nervous and hormonal control in speed and duration.
Describe homeostasis as keeping the internal environment constant.
Explain negative feedback around a set point.
Identify the skin structures involved in temperature control.
Describe the role of insulation in keeping mammals' body temperature constant.
Describe the roles of the hypothalamus and skin temperature receptors.
Explain how sweating, shivering, hair erection, vasodilation and vasoconstriction keep body temperature constant.
Explain why blood glucose concentration must be controlled.
Describe how the liver, pancreas, insulin and glucagon control blood glucose.
Describe signs and insulin treatment of Type 1 diabetes.
Describe gravitropism as growth toward or away from gravity.
Describe phototropism as growth toward or away from light.
Explain how auxin made in the shoot tip controls shoot growth by cell elongation.
Investigate gravitropism and phototropism in shoots and roots.

units.title: 16 Development of organisms and continuity of life

outcomes.text: Understand that chromosomes hold DNA carrying genes.
Describe haploid nuclei as having a single set of chromosomes.
Describe diploid nuclei as having two sets of chromosomes.
State that diploid cells have chromosome pairs, with 23 pairs in humans.
Describe mitosis as nuclear division giving genetically identical cells.
Outline the roles of mitosis: growth, repair, replacement and asexual reproduction.
Describe stem cells as unspecialised cells that divide and can then specialise.
State that meiosis produces gametes.
Describe meiosis as a reduction division giving genetically different haploid cells.
Understand that cancers result from uncontrolled cell division.
Describe asexual reproduction as one parent producing identical offspring.
Identify examples of asexual reproduction.
Describe sexual reproduction as fusion of haploid nuclei into a diploid zygote, giving varied offspring.
Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of asexual and sexual reproduction.
Identify and draw the parts of an insect-pollinated flower.
Identify and draw anthers and stigmas of a wind-pollinated flower.
Relate flower parts to their functions.
Compare insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers and their pollen.
Outline pollination and distinguish self-pollination from cross-pollination.
Discuss how self- and cross-pollination affect variation, adaptability and reliance on pollinators.
Describe pollen tube growth into the ovule and then fertilisation.
Understand that ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes a fruit.
Investigate and describe seed structure: embryo (radicle, plumule, cotyledons) and testa.
Understand that seed and fruit dispersal colonises new areas and lowers competition.
Relate features of wind-dispersed and animal-dispersed fruits to their functions.
Investigate the temperature, water and oxygen needed for germination.
Describe germination, including the role of enzymes.
Identify the male reproductive organs and describe their functions.
Identify the female reproductive organs and describe their functions.
Explain how sperm structure suits its function.
Explain how egg cell structure suits its function.
Describe fertilisation as fusion of the nuclei of sperm and egg.
Compare male and female gametes in size, structure, number and motility.
Describe the roles of testosterone and oestrogen in puberty.
Describe the menstrual cycle: egg release and changes in the uterus lining.
Explain how FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone control the menstrual cycle.
Describe early zygote development to an embryo implanting in the uterus.
State the functions of the amniotic sac and fluid.
Identify the placenta and umbilical cord and describe how they exchange substances between mother and fetus.
State that some viruses can cross the placenta and affect the fetus.
Describe variation as differences between individuals of one species.
Understand continuous variation as a range of phenotypes between two extremes.
Understand discontinuous variation as a few distinct phenotypes with no intermediates.
Understand that discontinuous variation is mostly genetic and continuous variation is genetic plus environmental.
Investigate and describe examples of both kinds of variation.
Describe DNA structure: double helix, nucleotide chains, bases A, T, C, G and base pairing.
Define a gene as a length of DNA that codes for a protein.
Explain that DNA controls cell function by controlling protein production, including enzymes.
State that gene base sequence sets the amino acid sequence of a protein.
Understand that amino acid sequence determines protein shape.
Describe inheritance as passing genetic information between generations.
Define an allele as an alternative form of a gene.
Use the terms dominant, recessive, phenotype, genotype, homozygous and heterozygous.
Use genetic diagrams and Punnett squares to predict monohybrid crosses and 1:1 and 3:1 ratios.
Explain why observed ratios often differ from expected ones, especially in small samples.
State that two identical homozygous parents breed pure.
Explain codominance using ABO blood groups.
Describe sex determination in humans (XX and XY).
Describe gene mutation as a random change in DNA base sequence, using sickle cell anaemia.
Describe chromosome mutation as a change in chromosome number or structure, using Down's syndrome.
State that mutation, meiosis, random mating and random fertilisation create genetic variation.
Understand that ionising radiation and some chemicals raise mutation rates.
Describe natural selection: variation, many offspring, struggle for survival, better-adapted survivors reproducing and passing on alleles.
Describe how a population's inherited features evolve through natural selection.
Describe antibiotic-resistant bacteria, including MRSA, as natural selection.
Describe artificial selection: choosing desirable parents, crossing them, selecting offspring and repeating over generations.
Describe the role of artificial selection in economically important plants and animals.
Explain the role of yeast in making bread and ethanol.
Understand that bacteria suit biotechnology because they reproduce fast and make complex molecules.
Discuss why bacteria are useful: few ethical concerns and plasmids.
Describe fermenters and the conditions controlled: temperature, pH, oxygen, nutrients and waste.
Describe enzymes in washing powders, pectinase in juice and lactase in lactose-free milk.
Describe genetic modification as removing, changing or inserting individual genes.
Understand that the human insulin gene was put into bacteria for commercial insulin.
Outline genetic modification of crops for herbicide resistance, pest resistance and extra vitamins.
Discuss potential advantages and risks of modifying crop plants and bacteria.

units.title: 19 Relationships of organisms with one another and with the environment

outcomes.text: Understand that the Sun is the main energy source for most biological systems.
Explain why most life depends completely on photosynthesis.
Describe energy flow through food chains and webs, ending in transfer to the environment.
Construct and interpret simple food chains.
Understand producer, consumer, herbivore, carnivore and decomposer.
Describe food webs as linked food chains and construct and interpret them.
Explain why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient.
Explain why food chains usually have fewer than five trophic levels.
Explain why eating crop plants is more energy efficient than eating livestock fed on crops.
Construct and interpret pyramids of numbers, biomass and energy.
Describe the carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, fossil fuels and combustion.
Outline the nitrogen cycle from decomposition to nitrification, fixation, plant uptake, protein, feeding and denitrification.
Outline the role of fungi and bacteria in decomposition.
Describe a population as one species living in one area at one time.
Describe a community as all the populations in an ecosystem.
Describe an ecosystem as a community and its environment interacting.
Describe biodiversity as the number of different species in an area.
State the factors affecting population growth: food, competition, predation and disease.
Understand that human population growth increases the demand for global resources.
Outline the causes and consequences of deforestation.
Describe the impact of over-harvesting and of introduced non-native species.
Describe how untreated sewage and fertiliser cause eutrophication, step by step, and the harm from greenhouse gases, pesticides and non-biodegradable plastics.
Discuss reasons for conservation: biodiversity, reducing extinction and protecting vulnerable environments.
Explain how forests are conserved by education, protected areas, quotas and replanting.
Explain how fish stocks are conserved by education, closed seasons, protected areas, net rules, quotas and monitoring.
Describe a sustainable resource as one produced as fast as it is removed.
